question: In bubble sort, which operation is primarily performed during a pass?

options.text: Comparing adjacent elements and swapping them if they are out of order
Selecting a pivot and partitioning the array
Counting the frequency of each key

explanation: Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements; a larger element moves toward the end during ascending sorting.

question: What is the worst-case time complexity of standard bubble sort?
explanation: In reverse order, bubble sort performs a quadratic number of comparisons and swaps.

question: When does optimized bubble sort achieve O(n) best-case time?

options.text: When the input is in reverse order
When the input is already sorted and a pass makes no swaps
Only when n is a power of two

explanation: A swap flag allows the algorithm to stop after a no-swap pass on sorted input.

question: For n distinct elements, how many comparisons does ordinary bubble sort make if it always completes all n−1 passes without early stopping?
explanation: The pass comparisons are (n−1)+(n−2)+…+1 = n(n−1)/2.

question: In selection sort in ascending order, what is done during each pass over the unsorted suffix?

options.text: The minimum element is selected and placed at the beginning of that suffix
The array is divided into two equal halves
The maximum element is moved to the end by adjacent swaps

explanation: Selection sort finds the minimum remaining element and swaps it into the next sorted position.

question: For an array of n elements, how many key comparisons does standard selection sort make regardless of the input order?
explanation: Selection sort scans each unsorted suffix, resulting in a fixed quadratic comparison count.

question: Which property is generally true of standard selection sort?

options.text: It performs O(n log n) comparisons on sorted input
It requires O(n) auxiliary array space
It performs O(n²) comparisons but at most O(n) swaps
It is stable by default in its usual swap-based form

explanation: Each pass makes at most one swap, so swaps are linear even though comparisons are quadratic.

question: In insertion sort, what happens to elements larger than the current key in the sorted prefix?

options.text: They are moved into a separate hash table
They are merged with the unsorted suffix
They are all swapped with the first element
They are shifted one position to the right

explanation: Insertion sort shifts larger prefix elements right to create a position for the key.

question: What is the best-case time complexity of insertion sort on an already sorted array?
explanation: Each element needs only a small constant number of checks when no shifts are required.

question: Which elementary sorting algorithm is typically adaptive and stable when implemented with the usual shifting method?
explanation: Insertion sort preserves equal-key order when it shifts only elements strictly greater than the key, and it is efficient on nearly sorted data.

question: After the first full pass of ascending bubble sort on [5, 1, 4, 2], what is the array?
In ascending selection sort on [4, 2, 5, 1], what is the array after the first pass?
explanation: The minimum value 1 is swapped with the first element 4.

question: Which statement best describes merge sort?

options.text: It divides the sequence into smaller parts, sorts them recursively, and merges sorted parts
It repeatedly selects the smallest remaining value using a full scan
It sorts only by swapping adjacent elements
It requires keys to be small non-negative integers

explanation: Merge sort follows divide-and-conquer: split, sort subproblems, and merge.

question: What is the worst-case time complexity of merge sort on an array of n elements?
explanation: There are O(log n) levels of splitting and O(n) total merge work per level.

question: What is a common auxiliary-space requirement of array-based merge sort?
explanation: Merging array segments typically uses temporary storage proportional to the number of elements.

question: Why can merge sort be stable?

options.text: It always swaps equal elements twice
It converts all keys to unique integers
During merging, equal keys from the left run can be taken before equal keys from the right run

explanation: Choosing the left item first on equality preserves the original relative order of equal-key records.

question: Quicksort primarily sorts by:

options.text: Partitioning elements around a pivot, then sorting the resulting subarrays
Repeatedly removing the minimum from a priority queue only
Merging two fully sorted halves using a temporary array
Counting the frequency of each possible key

explanation: Quicksort partitions around a pivot and recursively sorts the partitions.

question: What is the average-case time complexity of well-implemented quicksort with reasonably balanced partitions?
explanation: Balanced partitions produce logarithmic recursion depth with linear partition work per level.

question: What is the worst-case time complexity of quicksort?
explanation: Repeatedly highly unbalanced partitions can cause quadratic total work.

question: Which pivot choice can cause worst-case quicksort behavior on already sorted input for a common partition scheme?

options.text: Choosing a pivot near the middle by value
Always choosing the first or last element as pivot

explanation: On sorted data, an extreme endpoint pivot can repeatedly produce partitions of sizes 0 and n−1.

question: What is the purpose of partitioning in quicksort?

options.text: Place the pivot in its partition position and separate values according to the pivot rule
Count every key in a frequency array
Fully sort both halves before choosing a pivot
Guarantee that the entire array is sorted after one pass

explanation: Partitioning rearranges elements around the pivot; recursive calls complete the sort.

question: With consistently balanced partitions, the recursion depth of quicksort is approximately:
explanation: Each level reduces subproblem sizes by a constant fraction, giving logarithmic depth.

question: What is the worst-case recursion depth of quicksort when each pivot leaves one empty side and one side of size n−1?
explanation: The recursion then removes only one element per level, creating linear depth.

question: Heap sort uses which underlying structure?
explanation: Heap sort builds a max-heap for ascending order and repeatedly extracts the maximum to the end.

question: What is the worst-case time complexity of heap sort?
explanation: Building a heap is O(n), followed by n removals or root placements costing O(log n) each.

question: Which statement about standard in-place heap sort is correct?

options.text: It requires the input to be already sorted
It uses O(1) auxiliary array space and is not stable
It is stable and requires O(n) extra array space

explanation: Heap sort can be performed in place, but heap rearrangements do not preserve equal-key order.

question: Shell sort improves on insertion sort mainly by:

options.text: Using a count array for each key
Using a pivot to create two partitions
Initially comparing and moving elements separated by a gap, then reducing the gap

explanation: Shell sort performs gapped insertion sorts, with the gap eventually reduced to 1.

question: Which statement about Shell sort's complexity is most accurate?

options.text: It is always O(n log n) for every gap sequence
It always uses O(n) auxiliary space
Its time complexity depends on the chosen gap sequence

explanation: Different gap sequences yield different bounds; there is no single complexity independent of the sequence.

question: Which non-comparison sorting algorithm is especially suitable when integer keys lie in a small known range?
explanation: Counting sort counts occurrences of each key or key value in a bounded range.

question: If n items have integer keys in a range of size k, the typical time complexity of counting sort is:
explanation: Counting and outputting items takes time proportional to the number of items plus the key range.

question: A major limitation of counting sort is that:

options.text: It always has quadratic time complexity
It must compare every pair of elements
Its time and space can become large when the key range is huge relative to n
It can sort only linked lists

explanation: Counting sort allocates count storage based on the range of possible keys.

question: How does radix sort commonly process fixed-width integer keys?

options.text: It partitions only around a pivot
It merges arbitrary subarrays without considering digits
It repeatedly chooses the global minimum with comparisons
It sorts by one digit or position at a time using a stable sub-sort

explanation: Radix sort processes digits or positions in sequence; stable passes preserve earlier digit ordering.

question: Why is stability important in least-significant-digit radix sort?

options.text: Each digit pass must preserve the order established by less significant digits
It removes the need to examine digits
It ensures every pass runs in O(1)

explanation: A stable pass preserves prior ordering, allowing digit-wise results to combine correctly.

question: Bucket sort tends to work well when:

options.text: Input values are distributed fairly uniformly over a known range
All keys are arbitrary objects with no ordering
The input is guaranteed to be reverse sorted and buckets cannot be allocated

explanation: Uniform distribution can spread elements among buckets, making the expected bucket-level work small.

question: Which statement about comparison-based sorting is correct in the general comparison model?

options.text: It can always sort in O(n) comparisons
Its worst-case lower bound is Ω(n log n) for sorting arbitrary distinct keys

explanation: Decision-tree arguments establish an Ω(n log n) comparison lower bound for general comparison sorting.

question: Which algorithm is typically stable in its standard form?
explanation: A stable merge procedure takes equal keys from the left run first; standard merge sort can therefore be stable.

question: Which algorithm is usually adaptive in its common implementation, performing especially well on nearly sorted input?
explanation: Insertion sort makes few shifts and comparisons when the input is already or nearly sorted.

question: Which algorithm has O(n log n) worst-case time and is commonly used when a predictable comparison-sort bound is required?
explanation: Heap sort guarantees O(n log n) worst-case time, unlike basic quicksort.

question: For a stable sort of records by a secondary key followed by a primary key, which approach is generally valid?

options.text: Sort by the secondary key only
Randomly shuffle records between the two sorts
Stable-sort by the secondary key first, then stable-sort by the primary key
Use an unstable sort by the primary key first and discard the secondary key

explanation: A stable primary-key pass preserves the secondary-key order among records with equal primary keys.

question: Which algorithm's worst-case time can become quadratic because of repeatedly unbalanced partitions, even though its average case is O(n log n)?
explanation: Quicksort's partition balance determines its recursion depth and total work.

question: For n = 8 elements, how many comparisons does standard selection sort make?
explanation: Comparisons = n(n−1)/2 = 8×7/2 = 28.

question: For insertion sort on an already sorted array of n elements, how many element shifts are typically required?
explanation: No element is greater than the next key, so the standard insertion method performs no rightward shifts.

question: Which statement correctly compares merge sort and quicksort on arrays?

options.text: Merge sort always uses O(1) auxiliary space in standard array implementations
Both always have O(n) worst-case time
Merge sort has O(n log n) worst-case time; ordinary quicksort can have O(n²) worst-case time
Quicksort is always stable and merge sort is never stable

explanation: Merge sort maintains O(n log n) worst-case time, while quicksort's worst case depends on partition quality.

question: Which factor most directly affects the auxiliary stack space of recursive quicksort?

options.text: The number of distinct key values only
Whether the keys are integers or strings only
The number of swaps in bubble sort
The depth of its recursion tree

explanation: Stack space is proportional to recursion depth, which depends on partition balance.

question: Which is the usual best-case time complexity of merge sort?
explanation: Standard merge sort continues dividing and merging even if the input is already sorted.

question: Which sorting algorithm is non-comparison-based and can be stable when implemented with cumulative counts and output placement?
explanation: The stable counting-sort variant computes cumulative counts and places items into output in a way that preserves equal-key order.

question: Which statement about radix sort's complexity is generally accurate for d digit passes and n items, assuming each stable digit sort costs O(n + b)?

options.text: O(log n) for any key representation

explanation: Each of the d passes processes the items and digit alphabet/range, yielding O(d(n+b)).

question: Which property means that equal-key records retain their original relative order after sorting?
explanation: Stability preserves the relative order of records whose sort keys are equal.

question: Which algorithm is generally not adaptive in its standard form because it scans the remaining suffix even when the array is already sorted?
explanation: Selection sort still searches the full unsorted suffix to identify its minimum on each pass.

question: Which statement about the lower bound for comparison sorting and non-comparison sorting is correct?

options.text: Every sorting algorithm must make Ω(n log n) key comparisons
Counting and radix sort can beat the comparison lower bound by using assumptions about key representation or range
Non-comparison sorts work for arbitrary keys without constraints
Comparison sorting has no theoretical lower bound

explanation: The Ω(n log n) lower bound applies to comparison sorting; non-comparison methods exploit structure such as bounded integer keys.

question: For an ascending sort, a max-heap is commonly used by heap sort because:

options.text: The minimum is always at the root of a max-heap
A max-heap guarantees stable ordering of duplicates
The maximum can be repeatedly moved to the last position of the unsorted prefix
A max-heap stores all values in fully sorted order

explanation: The root of a max-heap is the maximum; swapping it to the end grows the sorted suffix.

question: Which sorting algorithm most directly benefits from an input that contains very few inversions?
explanation: Insertion sort's shifts are closely related to inversions, so nearly sorted inputs can be processed efficiently.

question: Which statement about bubble sort stability is correct for the usual implementation that swaps only when left > right?

options.text: It is stable because equal adjacent elements are not swapped
It is stable only if the array is reverse sorted
Stability cannot be defined for bubble sort
It is unstable because every pass swaps equal elements

explanation: Not swapping equal elements preserves their relative order.

question: What is a key trade-off of merge sort compared with in-place heap sort on arrays?

options.text: Both require the input to be sorted before running
Merge sort commonly needs O(n) extra space but is stable; heap sort is in-place but unstable
Heap sort is stable and merge sort is always unstable
Merge sort is always quadratic while heap sort is linear

explanation: Standard array merge sort uses auxiliary storage and can be stable; heap sort typically sorts in place but is unstable.

question: Which algorithm can be especially efficient when keys are small integers and the key range k is not much larger than n?
explanation: When k is reasonably small, O(n+k) counting sort can outperform comparison-based methods.

question: What is the typical worst-case time complexity of insertion sort?
explanation: Reverse-sorted input requires shifting many elements for each inserted key, producing quadratic work.

question: Which sorting algorithm generally has guaranteed O(n log n) time in best, average, and worst cases, but typically requires extra array storage?
explanation: Standard merge sort has O(n log n) time across cases and commonly uses O(n) extra array space.

question: Which statement about counting comparisons, swaps, and passes is correct for selection sort?

options.text: Its comparison count is O(log n)
It performs n−1 selection passes and about n(n−1)/2 key comparisons
It performs only one pass for any n

explanation: Each pass selects the minimum from the remaining suffix; comparison count is quadratic and there are n−1 passes.

question: For an array of n elements, how many passes are needed in the worst case by standard bubble sort?
explanation: A standard bubble sort needs at most n−1 passes; each pass places another largest remaining element at the end.

question: Which sorting algorithm is usually in-place, unstable, and has O(n log n) average time but O(n²) worst-case time?
explanation: Typical in-place quicksort is unstable, averages O(n log n), and can degrade to O(n²) with poor partitions.
